content.thinking:
Checking the timeline now: the monthly-spend flag was switched on at 03:10:18 by an admin, and the ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47 started around the same time. The flag was reverted at 03:17:15, but a P2 timestamp of 03:17:04 comes before it, which doesn't quite line up.

The logs show the error spikes landing in the same minutes the flag evaluated as on, even after the revert, so the revert may not have fully reached the service. ClientDisconnected errors were already present before onset, so they look like baseline noise rather than part of this incident.

Checking whether the revert actually reached the service: the error lines and the flag-on evaluations still line up in the same minutes after 03:17, so the rollback may not have fully taken effect. The 03:28 window also still shows flag-on evaluations alongside the errors, which is the main evidence for why the mitigation didn't stop the failures.

I'm working through the causal chain now: the account page errors trace back to ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47, starting around 03:10 when the monthly-spend flag was switched on, and I'm checking whether any deploys or earlier changes could explain it instead.

I'm weighing whether the revert counts as a refuted candidate for ruled_out, since the evidence still ties the errors to the flag being evaluated as on, and the record shows ZeroDivisionError only in those minutes.

I'm checking whether the revert really ended the harm: the record shows ZeroDivisionError only in minutes where the flag still evaluated on after the rollback, so the refutation tests the revert rather than the flag itself. I'll keep the flag in the causal chain, and I'm considering the deploy history as a candidate to rule out, though the record doesn't show an earlier change directly. Account pages rendered normally from 02:47 to 03:09, which suggests the running revision was healthy before onset.

I'm checking whether the mitigation actually reached the service: after the revert, the ZeroDivisionError lines still land in the same minutes where the flag kept evaluating as on, so the rollback may not have fully taken effect.

I'm tracing the last step of the chain: the flag-on path divides by a count of this month's purchases, which is empty for shoppers who bought before but not this month. That reading comes from one source only, so the link is still unverified, though it does reach a cause.

Now I'm laying out the causal chain's last step: the flag-on path runs a monthly average spend calculation that divides by this month's purchase count, which is likely zero for shoppers who haven't bought this month. I'm also noting that no pre-release check seems to have covered that case, which is the first contributing factor.

I'm now setting out the contributing factors: first, no check seems to have exercised the flag-on path for shoppers with no purchases this month before it went live, and second, the flag appears to have been switched on for all traffic at once with no staged rollout visible in the record.

Now I'm looking at whether the rollout itself was staged: the flag switched on for most account page evaluations within its first minute, with no gradual ramp or automatic rollback visible. I'm also checking whether an alert actually paged anyone, since it seems no on-call incident was linked to it.

I'm thinking about the last contributing factor: an alert that fired later than its evaluation window would explain, and whether anything in the record shows what caused that delay.

I'm weighing whether to include a contributing factor about the account page failing outright when the spend summary raises, rather than rendering without it. The record only shows the request failing, and the existing tests seem to expect that propagation, so I'm leaning toward leaving it out rather than claiming more than the record supports.

Next I'm drafting the action items: a pre-enable test requirement for flag-gated paths, a staged rollout for this kind of flag, an automatic halt when error rates climb after a flag change, and linking the error-rate alert to an on-call rotation so someone gets paged. I still need to find out what delayed the alert.

I'm drafting the write-up's remaining sections now: the switch-off should be confirmed at the service by checking that account page evaluations log the flag as off and the ZeroDivisionError stops, while I still need to work out why the earlier switch-off didn't take effect across every replica.

I'm checking whether the account page error warnings from 03:18 to 03:28 come from the same minutes as the ZeroDivisionError or from other errors, since that determines what level the Mitigation Agent actually saw. I'll keep the timestamps tied to their source lines rather than restating them.

Now I'm weighing what went well in the response: the investigator pinned the start to the minute of the flag change and named both the flag and the failing line early, and the mitigation agent's first move, reverting the flag, was reversible. Whether putting the flag back on later counts as a success or a failure is still open, since it restored the fault for all shoppers even though the record shows the revert had cut the on evaluations.

I'm weighing whether the Mitigation Agent's decision to switch the flag back on was right: after the revert, the ZeroDivisionError lines still appeared only in the minutes the flag kept evaluating as on, so putting it back meant every shopper hit the failing path again. I'm also noting that the Investigator's second pass tied the errors to the flag, yet Argus moved to fixing without retesting that link.

I'm noting two things that went wrong: the Mitigation Agent switched the flag back on after judging the revert refuted, even though the ZeroDivisionError lines had appeared only in minutes the flag was still evaluating as on, which put every shopper back on the failing path. The Investigator's second pass also said the errors follow the flag's evaluations, but that finding got counted as already tested for the first hypothesis, so the revert not fully taking effect was never checked.

I can't say what would have gone well beyond the early timing and the reversible first step, and I'm also treating the purchase-count divide-by-zero as Code-Fix's reading rather than something the record shows directly.

I'm settling on the root cause: with the flag on, the monthly average divides by this month's purchase count with no guard, so a shopper who bought earlier but not this month hits a ZeroDivisionError and the account page fails. I'm noting that this rests on the source Code-Fix read, since the deployment history doesn't say which revision the replicas actually run.

Checking how the root cause should be worded, I'm keeping the line number out of the plain-language summary and pointing to the file in the error log instead. The idea is that the monthly spending summary divides by this month's purchase count with no guard, so anyone who bought before but not this month hits the error and the account page fails.

Account pages could keep failing for shoppers who haven't bought anything this month, as long as the monthly spend feature stays on, which it was when Argus stopped. Shoppers' account page requests failed, and the service's overall error rate rose well above its usual level.

Now I'm tying the account page failures to the requests that were evaluating the monthly spend flag as on, starting from the minute the admin switched it on.

I'm working out the rule-outs now: a deploy or other change that could have caused this is ruled out only because the service looked healthy with the flag absent, and the change events show only the flag switch, with no deploy in between.

I'm ruling out the other flags next: the flag provider's history shows no flag change by anyone but Argus besides this one. I'm also noting that no test or check was seen exercising the monthly-spend path for a shopper with no purchases this month before the flag went on in production, and that the empty-month division would have been caught before shoppers reached it.

I'm listing the Investigator's correct early moves: it placed the onset at the minute of the flag change and named the flag and the failing file as its candidate. I'm also noting the Mitigation Agent's switch-off was reversible, so it could be tested safely, and the Code-Fix Agent's draft pull request was left for a person to review.

I'm checking what the mitigation agent did after the switch-off: it judged the revert refuted and turned the flag back on, even though the ZeroDivisionError only showed up in minutes when the flag was still evaluating as on. That put the account page back on the failing path. I'm also noting that Argus counted the switch-off as already tested and moved to fixing, even though the errors followed the flag's evaluations minute by minute, which hints the revert never fully took hold.

Working out the wording for the factor about the alert not being linked to on-call paging: nobody was paged, so a person could have stepped in when the switch-off failed to stop the errors and kept the flag off.

I'm noting how the Mitigation Agent's second switch-off went: it left the flag on, so the account page kept hitting the failing path, and the error level it saw came from the flag still being evaluated as on on some replicas.

I'm checking the last few details: the assumptions list is done, and I'm making sure the references and names are consistent throughout.

action_items.item: Before a feature flag on io-shop is switched on in production, require tests that run its flag-on path, including for shoppers with no purchases in the current period.
Roll out io-shop feature flags such as monthly-spend-feature in stages, by percentage of traffic, instead of switching them on for all traffic at once.
Halt a flag rollout on io-shop automatically, and turn the flag back off, when the account page error rate climbs after the flag change.
Link the ErrorRateSustained alert on io-shop to an on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.
Find out what delayed the ErrorRateSustained alert beyond what its evaluation interval, scraping allowance and onset minute account for, and remove that delay.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account page requests failed, and the service's error rate across all its requests rose far above its usual level.

Account page requests failed with ZeroDivisionError raised in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. This error was logged from the minute of onset onward, while before it account pages were logged rendering normally.

ruled_out.what: A deploy or other code change setting it off: the change events read back only the flag changes, all replicas ran the same revision, and account pages were logged rendering normally up to the minute before the flag was switched on.
Another flag change: apart from this one, the flag provider's history showed no flag change by anyone but Argus.

causal_chain.step: The requests reaching that code were the ones that evaluated monthly-spend-feature as on. Admin switched the flag on at {P1.1}, and from that minute the service logged it evaluating on for account page requests, alongside the errors.
With the flag on, the account page divides this month's spend by the number of the shopper's purchases this month, and that number is zero for a shopper who has bought before but not this month.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Switching on a new monthly spending summary on account pages sent shoppers into a calculation that likely divides by the number of things they bought this month, and that fails for anyone who has not bought anything yet this month.

contributing_factors.factor: No test or check was seen that ran the monthly-spend-feature path for a shopper with no purchases this month before the flag was switched on in production.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The empty-month division would have been found before any shopper reached it.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: The flag was not seen being rolled out in stages, and no automatic halt on rising errors was seen. In the minute it was switched on, most account page evaluations already read it as on.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A small share of shoppers would have hit the fault, and the rollout could have stopped before it reached most account page traffic.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: The ErrorRateSustained alert on io-shop was not linked to any on-call incident, so no person was paged.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A person could have stepped in when switching the flag off did not end the errors, and kept the flag off rather than leaving it switched back on.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

contributing_factors.factor: The alert fired {beyond_accounted_for} later than its evaluation interval, scraping allowance and onset minute account for. The record does not show what took the rest.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Argus would have started work on the incident sooner.
contributing_factors.label: CF-4

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent named the switch-on of monthly-spend-feature and the failing division in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py as its candidate cause.
The Mitigation Agent switched monthly-spend-feature off to test that candidate, an action that could be put back.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as a draft pull request, PR #543, for a person to review.

went_wrong: The Mitigation Agent judged the switch-off refuted and switched monthly-spend-feature back on. Yet after the switch-off, ZeroDivisionError was logged only in the minutes when the flag was still logged evaluating on ({G5309.4} and {Gce95.5}), so switching it back on put all account page traffic back on the failing path.

Argus counted C2 as already tested by the switch-off and moved to FIXING with nothing further to try. But C2 said the errors followed the flag's evaluations minute by minute, which pointed to the switch-off not having taken hold everywhere rather than to the flag being innocent.

input.root_cause: With monthly-spend-feature on, the account page works out the shopper's average spend per item this month by dividing this month's total by the number of purchases made this month, in `average_spend_per_item_this_month` in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. Nothing guards against an empty month, so a shopper who has bought before but not this month raises ZeroDivisionError and their account page request fails.
input.still_at_risk: With monthly-spend-feature back on, account pages could keep failing for any shopper who has bought before but not this month.
input.stops_the_harm: Switch monthly-spend-feature off again. To confirm it took effect, check at the service that account page requests log only monthly-spend-feature=off evaluations, with no monthly-spend-feature=on lines from any replica, and that ZeroDivisionError lines from src/io_shop/spend_summary.py stop appearing.
input.why_it_did_not_help: Find out whether switching monthly-spend-feature off reached every replica and every flag evaluation. After the switch-off the service still logged the flag evaluating on in {Gce95.5}, and ZeroDivisionError in the same minutes ({G5309.4}). Find what kept serving the flag as on, and whether the error level the Mitigation Agent saw came from those minutes or from other errors.
